sysd-scale-106.q: Why is a counter that reads its value, adds one and writes it back not linearizable, and how can it be fixed?
sysd-scale-106.a: Two processes can both read 0 and both write 1, so one increment is lost. An atomic compare-and-swap retried on failure, an atomic fetch-and-increment, or a lock around the critical section makes it linearizable.

sysd-scale-095.q: Under causal consistency, which writes must every process see in the same order, and which may be seen in different orders?
sysd-scale-095.a: Writes that are potentially causally related must be seen by all processes in the same order, while concurrent writes may be seen in a different order on different machines. Two writes are causally related when the processor doing the second write has just read the first.

sysd-scale-001.q: Why is two-phase commit called a blocking protocol?
sysd-scale-001.a: A participant that has voted Yes blocks until it receives commit or rollback, so if the coordinator fails permanently some participants never resolve their transactions.

sysd-scale-112.q: What makes one vector clock less than another, and what does that guarantee for events that happened before one another?
sysd-scale-112.a: VC(x) is less than VC(y) when every component of VC(x) is at most that of VC(y) and at least one is strictly smaller. If x happened before y, then VC(x) < VC(y).

sysd-scale-007.q: Why does the Google SRE book recommend renewable leases with timeouts rather than indefinite locks?
sysd-scale-007.a: Because they stop a crashed process from holding a lock forever.

sysd-scale-004.q: How does the pre-commit step of three-phase commit fix the ambiguity left by two-phase commit?
sysd-scale-004.a: The coordinator sends doCommit only after all participants have acknowledged they are prepared, so no participant can have committed before all know the decision.

sysd-scale-113.q: Why are atomic broadcast and consensus equivalent when processes can crash?
sysd-scale-113.a: Consensus reduces to atomic broadcast by proposing a value as a broadcast and deciding the first message received; the reverse runs consensus repeatedly on the next message.

sysd-scale-109.q: How many participants does it take to tolerate F Byzantine failures, compared with crash-only majority consensus?
sysd-scale-109.a: Tolerating F Byzantine failures needs at least 3F+1 participants, while majority-quorum consensus that tolerates only crashes needs just 2f+1 replicas for f failures.

sysd-scale-118.q: In Paxos, which value does the Proposer put in its Accept message once a quorum has promised?
sysd-scale-118.a: The value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported by the Acceptors, or the Proposer's own value if none was reported.

sysd-scale-119.q: In a consensus group, what does it signal when the term or view number rises fast, and what if it decreases?
sysd-scale-119.a: A fast increase signals a flapping leader, perhaps from network problems, and a decrease signals a serious bug.

sysd-scale-022.q: What happens in a leader election when a follower hears no heartbeat from the leader before its election timeout?
sysd-scale-022.a: It becomes a candidate: it increases the term counter, votes for itself and requests votes from all other servers, and a majority of votes makes it leader.

sysd-scale-026.q: What does Spanner's time API expose, and why does that matter?
sysd-scale-026.a: It exposes clock uncertainty, which is critical to external consistency, nonblocking reads in the past, lock-free snapshot transactions and atomic schema changes.

sysd-scale-028.q: How does a DynamoDB table keyed by a partition key plus a sort key differ from one keyed by a partition key alone?
sysd-scale-028.a: With a partition key alone, no two items can have the same partition key. With a sort key added, the partition key picks the physical location and the sort key orders items inside it, so items may share a partition key but not a sort key.

sysd-scale-031.q: Why does Cassandra not support multi-table JOINs, ad hoc aggregations or complex queries?
sysd-scale-031.a: Its distributed architecture optimizes for scalability and availability instead.

sysd-scale-120.q: What do the commit log and the Memtable each do when Cassandra takes a write?
sysd-scale-120.a: The commit log is a write-ahead log that ensures durability, and the Memtable is an in-memory structure sorted by primary key.

sysd-scale-121.q: How does ScyllaDB use a node's CPU cores differently from a design built on threads and shared memory?
sysd-scale-121.a: Each node is sharded per CPU core: each core handles a different subset of data, and the cores share nothing and communicate explicitly.

sysd-scale-041.q: Why should a MapReduce partition function spread keys roughly uniformly across reducers?
sysd-scale-041.a: A partition function sends each map output to a reducer, typically by hashing the key modulo the number of reducers; if the data is not spread roughly uniformly, the job waits on slow reducers.

sysd-msg-056.q: What happens to senders when the receiver of a message queue fails?
sysd-msg-056.a: Senders continue unaffected, because sender and receiver need not be online together; messages accumulate in the queue until the receiver restarts.

sysd-msg-050.q: When is at-least-once delivery good enough even though it can deliver the same message several times?
sysd-msg-050.a: When duplication is not a big issue or the consumer can deduplicate, for example by rejecting a duplicate write on a message's unique key.

sysd-msg-136.q: What does it mean that AMQP is a wire-level protocol, and why does that matter?
sysd-msg-136.a: It describes the format of the bytes sent across the network, so any compliant tool can interoperate with any other regardless of language, unlike API-level standards such as JMS.

sysd-msg-058.q: How does a dead letter queue keep the main queue moving?
sysd-msg-058.a: It sets aside messages that cannot be processed, so they can be inspected later without blocking processing or spending CPU cycles on a message that may never be consumed successfully.

sysd-msg-059.q: What do event streaming platforms give up in return for more scalability than message brokers?
sysd-msg-059.a: They cannot guarantee message delivery or track which consumers have received messages, and they offer fewer fault-tolerance features such as message resending and more limited routing and queueing.

sysd-msg-071.q: What does backpressure do for a queue, and what do clients see once the queue is full?
sysd-msg-071.a: Backpressure limits the queue size, which maintains a high throughput rate and good response times for jobs already in the queue. Once it fills up, clients get a server-busy or HTTP 503 status code to try again later.

sysd-msg-054.q: How does the claim check pattern handle large messages?
sysd-msg-054.a: It stores the whole payload in a database and transmits only a reference, which is later used to retrieve the payload.

sysd-msg-064.q: What does publish-subscribe add to the observer pattern?
sysd-msg-064.a: A broker, so publishers and subscribers are unaware of each other; it scales to distributed systems, filters by topic and isolates failures, whereas observer failures can affect the subject.

sysd-msg-065.q: How do topic-based and content-based filtering differ in pub/sub?
sysd-msg-065.a: With topic-based filtering, subscribers who register for a topic receive all messages published to it. With content-based filtering, subscribers define constraints on message attributes or content, and messages are delivered only if they match.

sysd-msg-066.q: Who receives each message in a pub/sub topic, and how does that differ from a message queue?
sysd-msg-066.a: In pub/sub all subscribers to the topic receive every message broadcast, while in a message queue each message is processed only once by a single consumer.

sysd-msg-043.q: How does Spark rebuild data that is lost?
sysd-msg-043.a: Its resilient distributed datasets are immutable and operations are lazy, so lost data is rebuilt from each RDD's lineage.

sysd-msg-038.q: What can go wrong if a Kafka consumer relies on auto-committing offsets?
sysd-msg-038.a: Auto-committing might acknowledge records before they are processed, so if the consumer goes down mid-processing, some records may never be processed.

sysd-msg-042.q: Why is transaction-log based change data capture attractive, and what makes it hard?
sysd-msg-042.a: It has minimal impact on the database, needs no application changes, and can replay the original transactions in the order they were committed. But no standard exists for log formats, most databases do not document them, and uncommitted changes later rolled back must be eliminated.

sysd-msg-020.q: How is a mistaken event corrected in an event-sourced system?
sysd-msg-020.a: Stored events are never changed, even erroneous ones; the only way to correct one is to add a new event with the new values.

sysd-msg-021.q: What is the difference between event sourcing and event-driven architecture?
sysd-msg-021.a: Event sourcing uses events as state, a different approach to storing data, whereas event-driven architecture uses events to communicate between service boundaries.

sysd-msg-030.q: How can an event-driven system avoid losing an event when a component crashes before handing it on?
sysd-msg-030.a: It persists in-transit events and dequeues them only after the next component acknowledges receipt, features known as client acknowledge mode and last participant support.

sysd-msg-024.q: What does CQRS separate, and why?
sysd-msg-024.a: It separates commands, which change the system and return only success or failure, from queries, which request information without changing state. The two play different roles, so each can be optimized as needed.

sysd-msg-034.q: Why do both short and long timeouts cause trouble in distributed systems, and which pattern helps?
sysd-msg-034.a: Short timeouts may fail legitimate requests prematurely, while long timeouts give slow error responses and a poor user experience. The circuit breaker pattern helps by monitoring service health, enabling faster failure detection.

sysd-msg-032.q: How can an event-driven system cope with event schemas that change across services?
sysd-msg-032.a: By versioning events, such as semantic versioning or schema evolution, to maintain backward and forward compatibility, and by using adapters that translate events between old and new formats.

sysd-msg-083.q: How does scaling differ between a monolith and microservices when only one function is constrained?
sysd-msg-083.a: A monolith supporting three functions must be scaled in its entirety even if only one is constrained, whereas with microservices only that function's service is scaled out.

sysd-msg-093.q: What are the data plane and the control plane of a service mesh?
sysd-msg-093.a: The data plane is the network proxies paired with each service, which intercept and process calls between services. The control plane is the set of management processes that coordinates the proxies and provides APIs to manipulate and observe the whole network.

sysd-msg-097.q: What is the main distinction between SOA and microservices?
sysd-msg-097.a: Scope: SOA defines how to make software components reusable through service interfaces and common communication standards, whereas microservices are many smallest independent service units aimed at team autonomy and decoupling.
